title: Tinkering Bench
strapline: Old clocks, keyboards and radios to take apart — real screwdrivers, real screws, and the deep pull of finding out how things work.
intent: Children satisfy a powerful curiosity — what is inside, how does it work, what happens if I undo this?
Children use real tools with genuine control — screwdrivers, spanners, pliers — for a real purpose.
Children develop the fine-motor strength and precision that unscrewing, twisting and levering demands.
Children reason and predict, forming theories about what each part does.
Children learn focus, patience and care, working slowly at a fiddly, absorbing task.
implementation: Source safe, gutted appliances to dismantle — old telephones, keyboards, clocks, radios (batteries and sharp parts removed, cords cut off).
Provide real child-sized tools — screwdrivers, spanners, pliers — and teach their safe, proper use.
Model the technique and the safety, then step back and let children work at their own pace.
Ask what each part might do and let children build their own theories before you offer any.
Sort the removed parts into trays so they become loose parts for building afterwards.
Keep it a slow, low-numbers area with clear rules — tools stay at the bench, goggles on.
Display the dismantled parts and photos, honouring the tinkering as real, serious work.
key_questions: What do you think is inside this one?
Which tool will help you undo that screw?
What do you think this part is for?
How does turning the screwdriver this way help?
What could we build with all the parts you've taken out?

impact.text: Children use real tools with intent and growing control for a genuine purpose.
Children develop fine-motor strength and precision through unscrewing, twisting and levering.
Children explore how things work — buttons, hinges, screws, mechanisms — and satisfy real curiosity.
Children ask real questions and form theories about what each part does.
Children stay focused and patient at a fiddly, absorbing task until it's done.
Children sort the salvaged parts and reuse them, building with what they've found.

enhancements: Safe gutted appliances — phones, keyboards, clocks, radios (made safe first).
Real child-sized screwdrivers, spanners and pliers on a tool board.
Safety goggles and a clear set of bench rules.
Sorting trays for the salvaged screws, cogs and parts.
A magnifying glass for inspecting the tiny mechanisms.
Clipboards for drawing and labelling what's inside.
A display of dismantled parts and 'how it worked' photos.

playing_exploring: Children follow a deep curiosity about the hidden insides of everyday things.
They explore real mechanisms hands-on, learning by taking apart.
active_learning: The fiddly, stubborn screw demands patience and persistence.
Children work slowly and carefully, absorbed for long stretches.
creating_thinking: Children form and test theories about what each part is for.
They reuse the salvaged parts inventively in new builds.
